y-m-24-01.title: If it worked for x=0 and x=1, does it work for every x?
y-m-24-01.topic: Calculating with letters: products of powers of the same letter, and counterexamples
y-m-24-01.goal: Judge whether checking that an expression works for a few numbers is evidence that it holds for all numbers, and make a counterexample yourself and explain which numbers make the two sides equal only by chance.
y-m-24-01.material: Sua said, "x²×x³ is x⁶!" (Reading: x squared times x cubed is x to the sixth.) Sua put 0 in for x and both sides were 0, and put 1 in for x and both sides were 1. In this task, x is a number from -5 to 5, and you may also put in decimals.
y-m-24-01.thinking.0: Judging what it means that an example passed
y-m-24-01.thinking.2: Explaining cases that hold by chance
y-m-24-01.prereq.0: The meaning of powers (example: x³ is x multiplied three times)
y-m-24-01.prereq.1: Finding the value of an expression by putting negative numbers and decimals in for a letter
y-m-24-01.s.s1.prompt: What can be said from Sua's check (both sides were the same for x=0 and x=1)?
y-m-24-01.s.s1.hint.0: First look at how the two numbers Sua put in, 0 and 1, differ from other numbers.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.hint.1: If you want to test Sua's statement, write down two or three numbers you would put in for x.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.o.a: Both sides were the same for x=0 and x=1, so we may conclude it holds for all x
y-m-24-01.s.s1.r.a: You turned two successes into 'it works for all numbers'. Even if a few examples work, that does not become 'all'.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.o.b: Both sides were the same for x=0 and x=1, but we do not yet know whether they are the same for other x
y-m-24-01.s.s1.r.b: This is the thinking of judging without going beyond the range the checked examples cover. Which x to put in next becomes important.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.o.c: Both sides were the same for x=0 and x=1, so we may conclude it always holds when x is positive
y-m-24-01.s.s1.r.c: You narrowed 'all' to 'positive', but you checked only one positive number, 1. Narrowing the range does not add evidence.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.o.d: Both sides were the same for x=0 and x=1, so evidence has appeared that Sua's statement is wrong
y-m-24-01.s.s1.r.d: You read the same result as evidence in the opposite direction. This check is not evidence that it is wrong either.
y-m-24-01.s.s1.explain: The fact that the two values were the same is confirmed only at those two values. To look for an example that breaks the statement, you need to test x other than 0 and 1.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different values of x for which x²×x³ and x⁶ have different values. (x is from -5 to 5)
y-m-24-01.s.s2.hint.0: Put 2 in for x and calculate x²×x³ and x⁶ separately.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.hint.1: If you come across a number that gives the same value, switch to another number and calculate. You can also try negative numbers and decimals.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make x a number from -5 to 5.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The values of x²×x³ and x⁶ are different. It is an example that breaks Sua's statement.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.fail.c2: For this x, the two sides are the same. It is not an example that breaks Sua's statement.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.explain: For example, if x=2, x²×x³=4×8=32 and x⁶=64, which are different. If x=-1, they are -1 and 1, and if x=0.5, they are 0.03125 and 0.015625, which are different. The only x for which the two sides are the same are 0 and 1, so Sua happened to pick exactly the two numbers that make them the same.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.prompt: Tell Sua. Write why they happened to be the same at x=0 and x=1, which Sua checked, and why they differ for other numbers.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.hint.0: You may bring over the x you found above and its calculation result and use them as they are.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write down for yourself what happens to the value when you take powers of 0 and 1.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.placeholder: Example: even if you take powers of 0 or 1, ... so ...
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write in your own words why putting in only 0 or 1 does not break the statement?
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you give at least one x that breaks the statement, with numbers?
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you distinguish 'they happened to be the same' from 'they are always the same'?
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.model.0: 0 and 1 stay 0 and 1 no matter how many times you multiply them, so both sides happened to be the same. If you put in 2, x²×x³ is 32 but x⁶ is 64, so they differ. So getting two right does not mean it is always right.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.model.1: They are the same only for x=0 and x=1, and different for other numbers. If x is 2, 4×8=32 and 2⁶=64, so they are not the same. x²×x³ is x multiplied five times and x⁶ is x multiplied six times, so the number of times it is multiplied differs.
y-m-24-01.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: The method that explains by the number of times x is multiplied is also good.

y-m-24-02.title: Bike rental plans: which is cheaper if you ride longer?
y-m-24-02.topic: Applying linear functions: comparing two fare expressions
y-m-24-02.goal: Revise your judgment in the order that data increases, and write a notice with conditions based on the time at which the fares of two linear expressions become equal.
y-m-24-02.material: A public bicycle rental station has two fare plans. Plan A has a base fare of 1000원 and adds 150원 for every minute, and plan B has a base fare of 400원 and adds 200원 for every minute. Riding time is counted in 1-minute units, and you can ride at most 60 minutes at a time. Let the riding time be x minutes and the fare be y원. I will give you the data one piece at a time.
y-m-24-02.thinking.0: Making a tentative judgment from partial data
y-m-24-02.thinking.1: Adjusting your confidence in a judgment with new data
y-m-24-02.thinking.2: Writing a conclusion with conditions attached
y-m-24-02.prereq.0: Putting numbers into a rule written as a linear expression to find the value
y-m-24-02.prereq.1: Understanding that the letter x stands for an amount in the situation, such as 'riding time (minutes)'
y-m-24-02.s.s1.prompt: Look at the data one piece at a time and judge which plan is cheaper. It is okay if your judgment changes.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of data, calculate and write the difference between A and B, and look at how that difference changes as the data changes.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.hint.1: If you come across a cell that does not fit your judgment, instead of changing your judgment, think about what condition would make it fit.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.info: This is part of the fare table. When you ride 0 minutes (paying only the base fare), A is 1000원 and B is 400원. When you ride 10 minutes, A is 2500원 and B is 2400원.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: If you looked at only these two lines, which plan would you say is cheaper when riding longer?
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.after: It is fine to predict from the shape that the difference is shrinking, as in c, and it is also fine to hold off on judging, as in d. But 'B stays cheaper' does not fit the fact that the difference is shrinking.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Even if you ride longer, B stays cheaper
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You looked only at the fact that B was cheaper in the two cells. You did not look at the fact that the difference between the two fares changed from 600원 to 100원.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The longer you ride, A stays cheaper than B
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You said the opposite even though the table shows cells where B is cheaper. Can you find a reason in the table?
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: B is cheaper now, but if you ride longer, A may become cheaper
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You read the shape of the difference between the two fares shrinking and carefully predicted the future change.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: There are only two cells, so we cannot say yet which is cheaper
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a careful judgment that admits the data is small. You can still use the change in the difference you can already see.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.info: A new fare has come out for 20 minutes. A is 4000원 and B is 4400원.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.after: B is cheaper at 0 and 10 minutes and A is cheaper at 20 minutes, so it fits the data to say the change happens between 10 and 20 minutes. If your first judgment was 'B stays cheaper for a bit longer', that part still carries over.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Keep the judgment that B is always cheaper
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You leave the first judgment as it is even though it does not fit the new data. It is a judgment that cannot explain the value at 20 minutes.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Somewhere between 10 and 20 minutes, which one is cheaper switches
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You read that the size order of the two reversed and guessed the interval where it switches.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You decided by looking at only the one cell at 20 minutes. B was cheaper at 0 and 10 minutes.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The 20-minute data seems to be written wrong, so keep the judgment so far
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Doubting the data itself is necessary, but you have no grounds for doubt. You can check with the expression whether the 20-minute fare is right.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.info: The fare rules are written as expressions on the store's notice board. A: y=1000+150x, B: y=400+200x. They say most users of this station ride between 8 and 15 minutes.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: How would it be good to advise people who ride 8 to 15 minutes?
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.after: At 12 minutes both A and B are 2800원. B is cheaper for less than 12 minutes and A is cheaper for more. If users ride 8 to 15 minutes, both sides of 12 minutes are included, so it is hard to advise just one way.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Advise based on 12 minutes. For less than that B is cheaper, and for more A is cheaper
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is the idea of putting values into the expressions to find the time at which the two fares become equal and splitting the advice before and after it.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You judged by the base fare only. You missed that the per-minute fare difference piles up as time grows.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You applied the result at 20 minutes as it is to 8 to 15 minutes. You did not check where the switch happens.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: There is no time when the two plans become equal, so advise that the fare is the same whichever you pick
y-m-24-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You wrapped it up without calculating whether there is a time when they are equal. You can find the time they are equal by putting values into the expressions.
y-m-24-02.s.s1.reflect: At first, with the data of two cells you could only say 'the difference is shrinking'. As the data grew, you learned that there is a point where it switches, and after the expressions were given you could state that point with a number. Point out which data changed your judgment and how.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different riding times x (minutes) for which plan A is cheaper than plan B. (x is a natural number from 1 to 60)
y-m-24-02.s.s2.hint.0: Put in several values for x and write the A fare and B fare side by side.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.hint.1: Increase the values and check whether A can become cheaper and then B cheaper again.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.ok.c1: It is from 1 minute to 60 minutes in 1-minute units.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make x a natural number from 1 to 60 (in 1-minute units).
y-m-24-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The A fare is cheaper than the B fare.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.fail.c2: At this time the A fare is not cheaper than the B fare. Calculate the two fares separately and compare them.
y-m-24-02.s.s2.explain: At 13 minutes A is 2950원 and B is 3000원. At 30 minutes A is 5500원 and B is 6400원. From 13 to 60 minutes A is always cheaper, at 12 minutes they are equal, and under 12 minutes B is cheaper.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.prompt: Write one or two sentences for the station's notice. Say which plan is better for people who ride 8 to 15 minutes, putting in the dividing time as a number.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.hint.0: First find and write the time at which the two fares become equal, and then write one line each for which is cheaper before and after it.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.hint.1: Put in 8 minutes and 15 minutes, compare the two fares, and check whether your sentence is right.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: If you ride longer than 12 minutes, ...
y-m-24-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check directly by putting values into the expressions that the dividing time is 12 minutes?
y-m-24-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you also think about exactly 12 minutes (they are equal)?
y-m-24-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write it divided by time instead of recommending only one plan?
y-m-24-02.s.s3.model.0: If you ride less than 12 minutes, plan B is cheaper, and if you ride longer than 12 minutes, plan A is cheaper. At exactly 12 minutes both are 2800원, the same.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.model.1: For people who will ride 8 to 11 minutes, B is cheaper, and for people who will ride 13 to 15 minutes, A is cheaper. At 12 minutes they are equal, so either is fine. If you do not know how long you will ride, the difference is small around 12 minutes, so B, which has the cheaper base fare, is less of a burden.
y-m-24-02.s.s3.modelNote.1: Choosing on the grounds that the difference is small is also possible.

y-m-24-03.title: The three friends' simultaneous equations: which one fits this problem?
y-m-24-03.topic: Setting up simultaneous equations: checking units and the meaning of letters
y-m-24-03.goal: Understand that there can be several simultaneous equations that describe the same situation, and check whether the units and the meaning of the letters fit, so that you can pick out an equation that does not fit without solving it.
y-m-24-03.material: A total of 10 adults and children entered an amusement park. The adult admission is 3000원 per person and the child admission is 2000원 per person, and the money paid is 24000원 in all. Let the number of adults be x and the number of children be y. (Reading: 3x is 'three x', 3000x is 'three thousand x'.) Three friends wrote this situation as simultaneous equations. 가: x+y=10 and 3000x+2000y=24000. 나: x+y=10 and 3x+2y=24000. 다: x+y=10 and 3x+2y=24. And there is also a friend who wrote 라: x+y=10 and 2000x+3000y=24000.
y-m-24-03.thinking.0: Picking out the ones that fit the situation from several equations
y-m-24-03.thinking.1: Checking that the units are consistent
y-m-24-03.thinking.2: Before solving, checking whether an equation is possible by its size
y-m-24-03.prereq.0: The meaning of simultaneous equations, and matching letters to quantities in a situation
y-m-24-03.prereq.2: Experience reading word problems with 2 unknowns
y-m-24-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose all the simultaneous equations that correctly describe the situation of this problem. (Judge by the meaning of the equations alone, without solving them.)
y-m-24-03.s.s1.hint.0: For each equation, write down one by one what unit the number in front of each letter and the number on the right are in.
y-m-24-03.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the adult fare is attached next to x in the equation, to fit the agreement that x is the number of adults.
y-m-24-03.s.s1.r.a: The adult fare is written as 3 for 3000원 while the total is written in won as it is, so units are mixed within one equation.
y-m-24-03.s.s1.r.b: This is the thinking that recognized that all amounts are written in units of thousand 원.
y-m-24-03.s.s1.r.c: All amounts are written in units of 원, and the values are multiplied to fit the meanings of x and y.
y-m-24-03.s.s1.r.d: The fares for adults and children are swapped. You did not look back at what x means.
y-m-24-03.s.s1.explain: 가 and 다 write the same situation in different units. Solving 가 gives x=4, y=6, and solving 다 gives the same answer. In 나, the 3 and 2 in 3x+2y are in units of thousand 원 but 24000 is in units of 원, so it does not fit, and in 라 the fares for adults and children are swapped so x=6, y=4 comes out and the numbers of adults and children are reversed.
y-m-24-03.s.s1.acc.0: 가 is right. Check whether 다 is also an equation that writes the same situation in units of thousand 원. Even if the units look different, they can describe the same situation.
y-m-24-03.s.s2.prompt: Write a way to show, without solving the simultaneous equations, that the second equation of 나, 3x+2y=24000, does not fit this situation.
y-m-24-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think about the largest value that the left side of the second equation of 나 can take, given x+y=10.
y-m-24-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare what unit the numbers 3, 2, and 24000 are each in.
y-m-24-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you write at least one reason that shows the equation is wrong without solving it?
y-m-24-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Can you say whether the reason you wrote is about 'units' or about 'size'?
y-m-24-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you also think of how to rewrite it, like 가 or 다?
y-m-24-03.s.s2.model.0: If x+y=10, then x and y are both 10 or less, so 3x+2y is at most 30. But it cannot be 24000, so 나 does not fit this situation.
y-m-24-03.s.s2.model.1: In 3x, the 3 is in units of thousand 원 but 24000 is in units of 원, so the units differ. If you write 3000x+2000y=24000 or change 24000 to 24, it becomes a correct equation.
y-m-24-03.s.s2.modelNote.1: It used units as the reason and even wrote how to fix it.

y-m-24-04.title: The solution for the number of drinks: where did it start to go wrong?
y-m-24-04.topic: Applying linear inequalities: interpreting 'less than' and 'at most'
y-m-24-04.goal: In a solution to an inequality word problem, find the line that goes against the meaning of the sentence, and explain with a numeric check how the answer changes when the wording of the condition changes.
y-m-24-04.material: Hyeonu wants to buy drinks to prepare for a school event. A drink costs 900원 per bottle, and the cooler box costs 3000원, paid just once. The teacher said, "Spend less than 12000원." Hyeonu let x be the number of drinks he buys and wrote his solution. (x is a natural number. Reading: 900x is 'nine hundred x', '<' means less than, '≤' means less than or equal to.)
y-m-24-04.thinking.1: Comparing answers depending on the wording of the condition
y-m-24-04.thinking.2: Checking the corrected solution by a numeric check
y-m-24-04.prereq.0: Expressing a situation with a linear inequality, and the meaning of the signs < and ≤
y-m-24-04.prereq.1: Reading the answer as a whole number in problems about counting natural numbers
y-m-24-04.s.s1.prompt: Pick the first line in Hyeonu's solution that goes against the meaning of the sentence.
y-m-24-04.s.s1.hint.0: Compare, one by one, whether each line has the same meaning as the line right before it.
y-m-24-04.s.s1.hint.1: Actually buy the number of bottles in the conclusion, work out how much is spent, and check whether it fits the sentence.
y-m-24-04.s.s1.line.0: If he buys x bottles of drinks, the money he spends is 900x+3000 (원).
y-m-24-04.s.s1.line.1: The teacher's words say to spend less than 12000원, so 900x+3000 ≤ 12000.
y-m-24-04.s.s1.line.4: Therefore he can buy at most 10 bottles of drinks.
y-m-24-04.s.s1.explain: In line 2, 'less than' was written as 'less than or equal to' (≤). 'Less' must not allow equal, so it has to be 900x+3000 < 12000. Lines 3 to 5 follow the inequality sign of line 2, so even though the calculation is right, the conclusion changed.
y-m-24-04.s.s2.prompt: If the teacher had said, "Spend 12000원 or less," what would happen to Hyeonu's solution?
y-m-24-04.s.s2.hint.0: Change the number of bottles to 9, 10, and 11, calculate the money spent, and write it in a table.
y-m-24-04.s.s2.hint.1: Mark how each amount of money relates to 12000원 with one of '<', '=', '>'.
y-m-24-04.s.s2.o.a: 9 bottles - even with 'or less', the number of bottles he can buy is the same
y-m-24-04.s.s2.r.a: You thought the answer is the same even if the word changes. You did not check whether the case of spending exactly 12000원 is included.
y-m-24-04.s.s2.o.b: 11 bottles - 'or less' allows one more bottle than 'less than'
y-m-24-04.s.s2.r.b: You memorized that 'or less' always allows one more. You can find out by checking how much is spent when you increase the number of bottles.
y-m-24-04.s.s2.o.c: 10 bottles - the case of spending exactly 12000원 is allowed
y-m-24-04.s.s2.r.c: This is the thinking that recognized that whether the word includes 'equal' can split the answer.
y-m-24-04.s.s2.explain: With 10 bottles, 900×10+3000=12000원, so it is allowed under 'or less'. With 11 bottles it is 12900원, which is over 12000원. So with 'or less' it is at most 10 bottles, and with 'less than' it is at most 9 bottles.
y-m-24-04.s.s3.prompt: Tell Hyeonu. In one or two sentences, write how to fix the wrong line and the numeric check you did to see that the corrected answer is right.
y-m-24-04.s.s3.hint.0: Rewrite the teacher's 'less than' with a single inequality sign.
y-m-24-04.s.s3.hint.1: Calculate the actual amount for the number of bottles in your corrected answer and compare it with 12000원.
y-m-24-04.s.s3.placeholder: Example: line 2 should be changed to ... Because ...
y-m-24-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you clearly write which line you changed and how, using the line number or the expression?
y-m-24-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate either 10 bottles or 9 bottles directly and compare it with 12000원?
y-m-24-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain in your own words the difference between 'less than' and 'at most'?
y-m-24-04.s.s3.model.0: Line 2 should be changed to 900x+3000 < 12000. Then x<10, so up to 9 bottles. If he buys 10 bottles, 9000+3000=12000원, which does not fit 'less'.
y-m-24-04.s.s3.model.1: 'Less' is a word that does not allow equal, so you must use < and not ≤. If he buys 10 bottles it is exactly 12000원, which is not allowed, and with 9 bottles it is 11100원, so it is at most 9 bottles.
y-m-24-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: It even checked the amount for 9 bottles.

y-m-24-05.title: If you know just one point, is the linear function determined?
y-m-24-05.topic: Equation and graph of a linear function: making equations that satisfy conditions
y-m-24-05.goal: Understand by making equations yourself that when conditions are lacking there can be several possible equations, that they become fewer as conditions are added, and that some conditions are impossible.
y-m-24-05.material: The graph of a linear function y=ax+b (a is a nonzero number) is a straight line. Jimin said, "If you only know that the graph passes through the point (2, 5), the equation of this linear function is determined as just one!" (Reading: the point (2, 5) is the point where y is 5 when x is 2. The x-intercept is the x-coordinate of the point where the graph meets the x-axis.)
y-m-24-05.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-24-05.thinking.1: Making several equations that satisfy a condition
y-m-24-05.thinking.2: Explaining the reason for an impossible case
y-m-24-05.prereq.0: What a and b in a linear function y=ax+b mean for the shape of the graph (level of the grade 8 linear function unit)
y-m-24-05.prereq.1: The meaning of the x-intercept and the y-intercept
y-m-24-05.s.s1.prompt: What do you think about Jimin's statement?
y-m-24-05.s.s1.hint.0: For a=1, b=3, put x=2 into the equation and check whether it passes through the point (2, 5).
y-m-24-05.s.s1.hint.1: Change a to other numbers, adjust b to match, and count how many equations that pass through the point come out.
y-m-24-05.s.s1.o.a: It is determined. From the coordinates of one point you can find both a and b
y-m-24-05.s.s1.r.a: You thought that one point lets you know both values a and b. You did not check how the two numbers of the point's coordinates relate to a and b in the equation.
y-m-24-05.s.s1.o.b: It is not determined. There is no linear function at all that passes through the point (2, 5)
y-m-24-05.s.s1.r.b: You thought no linear function passes through the point at all. You can find out by putting in a few a and b yourself and checking whether they pass through the point.
y-m-24-05.s.s1.o.c: It is determined. The point's coordinates are integers, so a and b are also integers and there is only one
y-m-24-05.s.s1.r.c: You thought that for a point with integer coordinates, a and b are also integers. Even if the coordinates are integers, a and b need not be integers.
y-m-24-05.s.s1.o.d: It is not determined. There are several pairs of a and b that pass through the point
y-m-24-05.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that looked at the relationship between a and b and read that there are several pairs.
y-m-24-05.s.s1.explain: To pass through the point (2, 5), the equation must hold when x=2 and y=5 are put in, so only one relationship arises between a and b. a and b are two numbers but there is one relationship, so there are several pairs. For example, (a, b)=(1, 3), (-1, 7), (5, -5) all pass through the point (2, 5).
y-m-24-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different linear functions y=ax+b that pass through the point (2, 5) and whose x-intercept is a positive integer. Enter suitable numbers for a and b. (You may write only numbers that can be written as decimals.)
y-m-24-05.s.s2.hint.0: If the x-intercept is fixed, the graph passes through two points, (x-intercept, 0) and (2, 5). Fix one x-intercept.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.hint.1: Once two points are fixed, work out a and b, and check by putting x=2 whether the point (2, 5) gives 5.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.ok.c1: a is not 0, so it is a linear function.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.fail.c1: To be a linear function, a must not be 0.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.fail.c2: When x=2 is put in, y does not become 5, so it does not pass through the point (2, 5).
y-m-24-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The x-intercept is a positive integer.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The x-intercept (the x when y=0) is not a positive integer. Put in y=0 and find x.
y-m-24-05.s.s2.explain: Let the x-intercept be p; then the graph passes through (p, 0) and (2, 5). y=5x-5 (x-intercept 1), y=-5x+15 (x-intercept 3), y=-2.5x+10 (x-intercept 4), and y=-x+7 (x-intercept 7) all fit the conditions. Besides these, you can make many more with fractional slopes.
y-m-24-05.s.s3.prompt: Is there a linear function y=ax+b that passes through the point (2, 5) and has x-intercept 2? Answer 'there is' or 'there is not' and write the reason.
y-m-24-05.s.s3.hint.0: Rewrite 'the x-intercept is 2' as the coordinates of a point (□, 0).
y-m-24-05.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the x-coordinate of that point with that of the point (2, 5).
y-m-24-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: if the x-intercept is 2, the graph must pass through the point ..., so ...
y-m-24-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you first write what the x-intercept 2 means about which point the graph passes through?
y-m-24-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you use as your reason that the same x would get two y values, or that 2a+b cannot be 0 and 5 at the same time?
y-m-24-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Is your reason concrete, using the numbers 2, 0, and 5?
y-m-24-05.s.s3.model.0: There isn't. If the x-intercept is 2, it passes through (2, 0), but it must also pass through (2, 5), so when x is 2, y would be two values, 0 and 5. For a linear function there must be exactly one y for each x.
y-m-24-05.s.s3.model.1: It is impossible. When you put in x=2, 2a+b would have to be 0 and 5 at the same time, which cannot happen. In the graph it would be the vertical line x=2, and that is not a linear function.
y-m-24-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: You can explain it either with the equation or with the shape of the graph.

y-m-24-06.title: The sum of four squares on a calendar: how far is Jiyun's statement right?
y-m-24-06.topic: Expressions with letters: explaining the sum of numbers on a calendar
y-m-24-06.goal: Revise a rule built from a few examples using new data, set up an expression with letters to check under what condition the rule holds, and then make examples for another condition in the same way.
y-m-24-06.material: A calendar has 7 squares in a row (Sun to Sat), this month has 31 days, and the 1st is a Sunday. So the 1st to 7th are the first row and the 8th to 14th are the second row. If you pick a 2×2 block of squares (2 squares across and 2 squares down) on this calendar, you get four numbers. Jiyun said, "If you add the four numbers of a 2×2 block, it's always a multiple of 8!"
y-m-24-06.thinking.0: Evaluating a rule made from examples
y-m-24-06.thinking.1: Revising a rule with conditions using new data
y-m-24-06.thinking.2: Finding the condition with an expression in letters
y-m-24-06.prereq.0: Experience of writing a situation as an expression using letters (example: writing consecutive numbers as a, a+1)
y-m-24-06.prereq.1: The meaning of multiples and of even and odd numbers
y-m-24-06.s.s1.prompt: Test Jiyun's statement along with new data.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of data, mark whether the number in the upper-left square is even or odd.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.hint.1: If data comes up that does not fit your judgment, calculate once more to check, and then decide how to revise your judgment.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.info: Jiyun tested three times. If the upper-left square is the 2nd, add 2, 3, 9, 10 to get 24. If it is the 10th, add 10, 11, 17, 18 to get 56. If it is the 12th, add 12, 13, 19, 20 to get 64. All three times it is a multiple of 8.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.ask: How much can you trust Jiyun's statement ('always a multiple of 8')?
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.after: The three examples support the rule, but there is no guarantee that the same rule holds at every position. It is also worth noticing that the upper-left squares were 2, 10, and 12 (all even).
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.o.a: It was right all three times, so we can trust that it always holds
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You turned three checks into 'always'. You did not look at what kind of positions were tested.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.o.b: It seems right, but only three positions were tested, so it is too early to be sure
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You recognized that examples support a rule but are not a proof.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The sums are all different, 24, 56, 64, so it is not a rule but a coincidence
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You decided it is not a rule because the values of the sums differ. Even though the values differ, they have something in common: all are multiples of 8.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.o.d: I cannot judge yet, so I want to test other positions too
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a judgment that sees the examples as lacking and tries to find new data.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.info: Minseo tested other positions. If the upper-left square is the 1st, add 1, 2, 8, 9 to get 20. If it is the 3rd, add 3, 4, 10, 11 to get 28.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.ask: What should be done with Jiyun's statement now?
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.after: 20 and 28 are not multiples of 8, so 'always' is broken. But it was right for even squares, so both paths, dropping the rule or fixing it by adding a condition, are reasonable.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.o.a: 20 and 28 are not multiples of 8, so 'always a multiple of 8' does not hold
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You recognized the power of a counterexample: if even one example breaks a rule, 'always' does not hold.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 20 and 28 may have been calculated wrongly, so leave Jiyun's statement as it is
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You blamed the new data on a calculation mistake. You can easily recheck by adding the four numbers in both blocks.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.o.c: If you add the condition 'only when the upper-left square is even', Jiyun's statement can be saved
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.r.c: This is the idea of not dropping the rule but fixing it by narrowing the range in which it holds.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.o.d: There are only two, so Jiyun's statement cannot be dropped yet
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.1.r.d: A single counterexample breaks 'always', but you put it off because there are few of them.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.info: If the number in the upper-left square is a, the four numbers are a, a+1, a+7, a+8, and the sum is 4a+16.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.ask: What can you say with this expression?
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.after: 4a+16=4(a+4), so it is always a multiple of 4. It becomes a multiple of 8 only when a+4 is even, that is, only when a is even. Jiyun's statement is right if you add the condition 'when the upper-left square is even'.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Whatever a is, the sum is a multiple of 8. Jiyun's statement is confirmed with letters
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You said it is a multiple of 8 by looking only at the surface of the expression. It does not fit the fact that the sum 20, which is not a multiple of 8, came out earlier.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.o.b: The sum is 4a+16, so the bigger a is, the closer it gets to a multiple of 8
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You mixed up a getting bigger with whether it is a multiple. Being a multiple is decided not by size but by whether it divides evenly.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Whatever a is, the sum is a multiple of 4, and whether it is a multiple of 8 depends on a
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a judgment that read the expression as 4×(a+4) and connected it with the earlier data (only the even cases are multiples of 8).
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The expression contains a, so we cannot tell what multiple it is
y-m-24-06.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You thought nothing can be said when there is a letter. If you factor the expression, you can see the factor that is always in it.
y-m-24-06.s.s1.reflect: With three examples you could only say it 'seems right'. When a counterexample came out, 'always' was broken, and with the expression in letters you could see under what condition it holds. Point out at which step your judgment changed.
y-m-24-06.s.s2.prompt: On the same calendar, find and enter 3 different numbers a for the upper-left square such that the sum of the four numbers in the 2×2 block is a multiple of 12. (a is a natural number from 1 to 23, and a Saturday square like the 7th, 14th, or 21st cannot be the upper-left one.)
y-m-24-06.s.s2.hint.0: Fix one a and add the four numbers a, a+1, a+7, a+8 yourself to see whether the sum is a multiple of 12.
y-m-24-06.s.s2.hint.1: Using the expression for the sum found earlier, look at the expression and work out how a must be chosen to make it a multiple of 12.
y-m-24-06.s.s2.var.a: The number in the upper-left square
y-m-24-06.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a number that makes a 2×2 block inside the calendar.
y-m-24-06.s.s2.fail.c1: a must be a natural number from 1 to 23.
y-m-24-06.s.s2.ok.c2: It is not a Saturday square.
y-m-24-06.s.s2.fail.c2: A multiple of 7 is a Saturday square, so the square to its right wraps to the next row. It cannot be the upper-left square.
y-m-24-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The sum of the four numbers is a multiple of 12.
y-m-24-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of the four numbers is not a multiple of 12. Add the four numbers yourself.
y-m-24-06.s.s2.explain: The sum is 4a+16=4(a+4), so if a+4 is a multiple of 3, the sum is a multiple of 12. The a that fit are 2, 5, 8, 11, 17, 20, 23. 14 also has a+4=18, a multiple of 3, but it is a Saturday square so it cannot be used.

y-m-24-07.title: If candies are shared out, how many students are there?
y-m-24-07.topic: Applying linear inequalities: finding possible cases from conditions given as a range
y-m-24-07.goal: Understand that when a condition is given as a range the answer may not be settled as one, find all the possible cases, and then say what more you need to know to settle on one.
y-m-24-07.material: You want to hand out candies to x classmates. There are y candies in all. One way is to give 4 candies each, which leaves 3 candies. Another way is to give 5 candies each, where every student except the last one gets 5 and the last student gets at least 1 and at most 4. (x is a natural number that is at least 2.)
y-m-24-07.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-24-07.thinking.1: Finding possible cases within a range condition
y-m-24-07.thinking.2: Suggesting the extra information that is needed
y-m-24-07.prereq.0: The meaning of a linear inequality, and finding natural numbers that fit the conditions
y-m-24-07.s.s1.prompt: Is the number of students x settled as one value by these conditions alone?
y-m-24-07.s.s1.hint.0: Put in a value for x, like 3, 4, or 5, and find how many candies there are.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.hint.1: With that number of candies, calculate how many the last student gets when 5 each are given out.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.o.a: It is not settled. The last student's share can vary between 1 and 4
y-m-24-07.s.s1.r.a: You read that the last student's share is given not as one number but as a range.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.o.b: It is settled as one. 4x+3 and 5x have to be equal, so x is just one
y-m-24-07.s.s1.r.b: You set the two counts equal, as in a 'short' problem. In this problem the last student does not get a full 5, so it cannot be said to equal 5x.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.o.c: We cannot know. Because we do not know how many candies there are in all
y-m-24-07.s.s1.r.c: You thought that not knowing the number of candies is the obstacle. The number of candies is connected to x through the expression for giving 4 each.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.o.d: It is not settled. Whatever the number of candies, the number of students can be chosen freely
y-m-24-07.s.s1.r.d: You thought the conditions hardly limit the number of students. You did not work out how each condition limits x.
y-m-24-07.s.s1.explain: Between the number of students and the number of candies there are two conditions: 'giving 4 each leaves 3' and 'the last student gets 1 to 4'. You have to work out directly whether one x or several x fit these conditions. In the next step, make the possible cases and check.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.prompt: Find and enter 3 different pairs (number of students x, number of candies y) that satisfy both conditions. (If you give 4 each, 3 are left over, and if you give 5 each, the last student gets at least 1 and at most 4.)
y-m-24-07.s.s2.hint.0: Fix the number of students x, find the number of candies y, and then calculate how many candies are left after giving 5 each to x-1 students.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.hint.1: Change x one at a time, write in a table how many candies are left over, and look at the range in which the condition is satisfied.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of students is a natural number that is at least 2.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be a natural number that is at least 2.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.ok.c2: If you give 4 each, 3 are left.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.fail.c2: This does not fit the condition that 3 are left over when giving 4 each. Add the 3 left over to the 4 each given to x students.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.ok.c3: Even when giving 5 each, the last student gets at least 1 and at most 4.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.fail.c3: When giving 5 each, the candies the last student gets are not between 1 and 4. Check the number left after giving 5 each to (x-1) students.
y-m-24-07.s.s2.explain: The possible cases are (4, 19), (5, 23), (6, 27), (7, 31), four in all. For example, with 6 students there are 27 candies, and if you give 5 each to 5 students, 25 candies, the last student gets 2. With 3 students the last student would also get 5, and with 8 students the last student gets 0, so they do not fit the conditions.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.prompt: What one more piece of information could be given to settle the number of students as exactly one value? Write that information as a number, and also write the number of students in that case.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.hint.0: Write side by side the number of candies and the number the last student gets for the four possible cases.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.hint.1: Find in the table the value that tells the four cases apart.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: if you are told the last student got ... candies, there are ... students.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you check that the information you chose leaves just one of the four possible cases?
y-m-24-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you calculate the number of students with the information you chose and check that it is right?
y-m-24-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether it could be settled as one by other information too?
y-m-24-07.s.s3.model.0: If you tell us the last student got 3 candies, the students are settled as 5.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.model.1: If you tell us there are 27 candies in all, take away the 3 left over when giving 4 each and divide the 24 candies by 4, so there are 6 students.
y-m-24-07.s.s3.modelNote.1: The method of giving the number of candies also works.
